claim: Micromeres are unique to echinoids among echinoderms.
source: Micromere formation in the sea urchin embryo is a highly controlled ACD event since this cell lineage undergoes autonomous cell specification and functions as organizers as soon as it is formed at the 16-cell stage (Hörstadius, 1928; Ransick and Davidson, 1993).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature (Hörstadius, 1928; Ransick and Davidson, 1993) to support the claim about micromere formation and function.

claim: Micromeres autonomously divide asymmetrically to produce large and small micromeres at the 32-cell stage.
source: For example, micromeres autonomously divide asymmetrically again to produce large and small micromeres that are committed to two specific lineages, forming skeletogenic cells and the germline, respectively, at the 32-cell stage (Okazaki, 1975; Yajima and Wessel, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Okazaki, 1975; Yajima and Wessel, 2011).

claim: Large micromeres form skeletogenic cells and small micromeres form the germline.
source: For example, micromeres autonomously divide asymmetrically again to produce large and small micromeres that are committed to two specific lineages, forming skeletogenic cells and the germline, respectively, at the 32-cell stage (Okazaki, 1975; Yajima and Wessel, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Okazaki, 1975; Yajima and Wessel, 2011).

claim: Early segregation of the germline is unique to sea urchins among echinoderms.
source: This early segregation of the germline is unique to sea urchins among echinoderms (Juliano and Wessel, 2009; Fresques et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Juliano and Wessel, 2009; Fresques et al., 2016).

claim: Micromeres induce endomesoderm specification even when placed in ectopic regions of the embryo.
source: Further, micromeres induce endomesoderm specification (e.g., gastrulation) even when they are placed in the ectopic region of the embryo, such as the animal cap, suggesting they function as a major signaling center in this embryo (Hörstadius, 1928; Ransick and Davidson, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Hörstadius, 1928; Ransick and Davidson, 1993).

claim: Removal of sea urchin micromeres results in compromised or delayed endomesoderm development.
source: The removal of sea urchin micromeres results in compromised or delayed endomesoderm development and compensatory upregulation of a germline factor, Vasa, to presumably start over the developmental program (Ransick and Davidson, 1993; Voronina and Wessel, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Ransick and Davidson, 1993; Voronina and Wessel, 2006).

claim: Removal of sea urchin micromeres results in compensatory upregulation of Vasa.
source: The removal of sea urchin micromeres results in compromised or delayed endomesoderm development and compensatory upregulation of a germline factor, Vasa, to presumably start over the developmental program (Ransick and Davidson, 1993; Voronina and Wessel, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Ransick and Davidson, 1993; Voronina and Wessel, 2006).

claim: In sea star embryos, removal of smaller cells does not impact embryonic patterning.
source: For example, in sea star embryos, the removal of smaller cells does not impact embryonic patterning, and unequal cell divisions do not appear to be linked to specific cell fate regulation or function (Barone et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Barone et al., 2022).

claim: Sea urchins diverged relatively later from the common ancestor of echinoderms.
source: Fossil records and phylogenetic tree analysis suggest that sea urchins diverged relatively later from the common ancestor of echinoderms (Bottjer et al., 2006; Wada and Satoh, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Bottjer et al., 2006; Wada and Satoh, 1994).

claim: Micromeres are considered to have emerged later during echinoderm diversification.
source: Since micromeres are unique to echinoids (sea urchins, sand dollars, pencil urchins), they are considered to have emerged later during echinoderm diversification, which has dramatically changed the developmental style in the sea urchin embryo (Emura and Yajima, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Emura and Yajima, 2022).

claim: SpAGS localizes to the vegetal cortex before and during micromere formation.
source: In the sea urchin (Strongylocentrotus purpuratus; Sp), SpAGS localizes to the vegetal cortex before and during micromere formation, and its knockdown inhibits micromere formation (Poon et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Poon et al., 2019).

claim: SpAGS knockdown inhibits micromere formation.
source: In the sea urchin (Strongylocentrotus purpuratus; Sp), SpAGS localizes to the vegetal cortex before and during micromere formation, and its knockdown inhibits micromere formation (Poon et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Poon et al., 2019).

claim: PmAGS shows no cortical localization during early embryogenesis in sea star.
source: On the other hand, in the sea star (Patiria miniata; Pm), PmAGS shows no cortical localization nor any significant role in ACD during early embryogenesis.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: PmAGS has no significant role in ACD during early embryogenesis in sea star.
source: On the other hand, in the sea star (Patiria miniata; Pm), PmAGS shows no cortical localization nor any significant role in ACD during early embryogenesis.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: The pencil urchin diverged around 252 million years ago.
source: The pencil urchin (Eucidaris tribuloides; Et) is an ancestral type of sea urchin that diverged around 252 million years ago, located between the sea star and the sea urchin on the phylogenetic tree.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: Pencil urchin embryos stochastically form 0 to 4 micromere-like cells.
source: It stochastically forms 0 to 4 micromere-like cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B showing the stochastic formation of micromere-like cells.

claim: EtAGS localizes to the vegetal cortex only when pencil urchin embryos form micromere-like cells.
source: In these embryos, EtAGS localizes to the vegetal cortex only when the embryos form micromere-like cells (Poon et al., 2019), suggesting a close correlation between cortical AGS localization and micromere-like cell formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Poon et al., 2019).

claim: Introduction of sea urchin AGS into sea star embryos induces random unequal cell divisions.
source: Furthermore, the introduction of sea urchin AGS into sea star embryos induces random unequal cell divisions by recruiting the spindle poles to the cortex (Poon et al., 2019), suggesting that SpAGS facilitates unequal cell divisions even in other echinoderm species.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Poon et al., 2019).

claim: AGS orthologs increased functional motif numbers over the course of evolution.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of AGS orthologs across taxa suggests that AGS orthologs increased the functional motif numbers over the course of evolution, likely allowing additional molecular interactions and mechanisms to modulate ACD in a more nuanced manner in higher-order organisms (Wavreil and Yajima, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Wavreil and Yajima, 2020).

claim: Mouse LGN can substitute for Drosophila Pins in Drosophila cells.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, indeed, prior studies suggest that the higher-order mouse AGS ortholog (LGN) can substitute for its fly ortholog (Pins) in Drosophila cells, while the basal-order fly Pins cannot substitute its chick ortholog function in chicks, the higher-order organism (Yu et al., 2003; Saadaoui et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Yu et al., 2003; Saadaoui et al., 2017).

claim: Drosophila Pins cannot substitute for its chick ortholog function in chicks.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, indeed, prior studies suggest that the higher-order mouse AGS ortholog (LGN) can substitute for its fly ortholog (Pins) in Drosophila cells, while the basal-order fly Pins cannot substitute its chick ortholog function in chicks, the higher-order organism (Yu et al., 2003; Saadaoui et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Yu et al., 2003; Saadaoui et al., 2017).

claim: AGS consists of two functional domains: N-terminus with TPR motifs and C-terminus with GoLoco motifs.
source: AGS consists of two functional domains: the N-terminus contains tetratricopeptide repeats (TPR) and the C-terminus contains G-protein regulatory motifs (GoLoco, GL) (Bernard et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Bernard et al., 2001).

claim: AGS switches between closed and open structures based on intramolecular interaction between TPR and GL motifs.
source: AGS switches between a closed and open structure based on the intramolecular interaction between the TPR and GL motifs (Du and Macara, 2004; Johnston et al., 2009; Nipper et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Du and Macara, 2004; Johnston et al., 2009; Nipper et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2013).

claim: TPR motifs regulate protein-protein interaction with partners such as inscuteable and NuMA.
source: The TPR motifs regulate protein–protein interaction with various partners such as inscuteable (Insc) for its proper cortical localization or nuclear mitotic apparatus (NuMA) for its microtubule-pulling force generation.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: GL motifs interact with Gαi for anchoring to the cortex.
source: In contrast, the GL motifs interact with the heterotrimeric G-protein subunit Gαi for its anchoring to the cortex (Bowman et al., 2006; Culurgioni et al., 2011; Culurgioni et al., 2018; Du and Macara, 2004; Parmentier et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Bowman et al., 2006; Culurgioni et al., 2011; Culurgioni et al., 2018; Du and Macara, 2004; Parmentier et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2000).

claim: Pins/LGN generally remain in the autoinhibited form in the cell.
source: Studies investigating AGS mechanisms in fly and mammals reveal that Pins/LGN (AGS orthologs) generally remain in the autoinhibited form in the cell (Du and Macara, 2004; Johnston et al., 2009; Nipper et al., 2007; Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Du and Macara, 2004; Johnston et al., 2009; Nipper et al., 2007) and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Insc recruits Pins/LGN to the cortex during ACD.
source: At the time of ACD, Insc recruits Pins/LGN to the cortex, which is then established and maintained there through Gαi interaction for the subsequent steps.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text based on established knowledge.

claim: Gαi-binding releases Pins/LGN from autoinhibition.
source: This Gαi-binding releases Pins/LGN from its autoinhibition and allows it to interact with NuMA, which recruits the motor protein dynein to generate pulling forces on the microtubules and facilitate ACD (Bowman et al., 2006; Culurgioni et al., 2011; Izumi et al., 2006; Parmentier et al., 2000; Schaefer et al., 2001; Siller et al., 2006; Williams et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2000; Yuzawa et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Bowman et al., 2006; Culurgioni et al., 2011; Izumi et al., 2006; Parmentier et al., 2000; Schaefer et al., 2001; Siller et al., 2006; Williams et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2000; Yuzawa et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2011).

claim: AGS-1F and Full AGS exhibit vegetal cortex-specific localization.
source: Embryos injected with full-length SpAGS (Full AGS) or AGS-1F exhibited vegetal cortex-specific localization.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: AGS-2F and AGS-3F show uniform cortical localization.
source: In contrast, AGS-2F and AGS-3F showed uniform cortical localization (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: TPR4-6 is necessary for restricting AGS to the vegetal cortex.
source: These results suggest that TPR4-6 is necessary for restricting AGS to the vegetal cortex, whereas TPR1-3 appears to play a less critical role in controlling AGS localization.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing differential localization of TPR deletion mutants.

claim: TPR1-3 plays a less critical role in controlling AGS localization.
source: These results suggest that TPR4-6 is necessary for restricting AGS to the vegetal cortex, whereas TPR1-3 appears to play a less critical role in controlling AGS localization.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing differential localization of TPR deletion mutants.

claim: AGS-3F injection prevents normal micromere formation.
source: Since none of the AGS-3F-injected embryos formed normal micromeres, 'micromere-like cells' were counted based on their vertical cell division, not relative to their size.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: AGS-2F and AGS-3F dramatically compromised development with incomplete skeleton extension or gut formation.
source: The AGS-1F mutant mostly showed normal development with extended skeletal rods, whereas AGS-2F and AGS-3F dramatically compromised development with incomplete skeleton extension or gut formation (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: N-terminal TPR deletions cause a dominant negative phenotype.
source: Since these N-terminal deletions appear to cause a dominant negative phenotype, we did not knock down endogenous SpAGS in these experiments.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: The N-terminal TPR domain is necessary to restrict SpAGS localization at the vegetal cortex.
source: These results suggest that the N-terminal TPR domain is necessary to restrict SpAGS localization at the vegetal cortex.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing localization patterns of TPR deletion mutants.

claim: The SpAGS C-terminus is sufficient to control Gαi localization at the vegetal cortex.
source: Notably, Gαi localization was also recruited to the exact ectopic location as AGS-2F and -3F mutants (Figure 2I), suggesting that the SpAGS C-terminus is sufficient to control the Gαi localization at the vegetal cortex.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Protein sequences of AGS orthologs across echinoderms are almost identical in their N-termini.
source: Protein sequences of AGS orthologs across echinoderms are almost identical in their N-termini, suggesting that the AGS N-terminus serves as a core functional domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The AGS C-terminus appears highly variable across echinoderms.
source: In contrast, the AGS C-terminus appears highly variable across echinoderms.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: SpAGS mutants missing GL1, GL3, or all GL motifs failed to localize at the vegetal cortex.
source: SpAGS mutants missing GL1 (ΔGL1), GL3 (ΔGL3), or all GL motifs (ΔGL1-4) failed to localize at the vegetal cortex compared to the Full AGS control (Figure 3B–D), suggesting that GL1 and GL3 are essential for cortical localization of AGS.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3B–D.

claim: GL1 and GL3 are essential for cortical localization of AGS.
source: SpAGS mutants missing GL1 (ΔGL1), GL3 (ΔGL3), or all GL motifs (ΔGL1-4) failed to localize at the vegetal cortex compared to the Full AGS control (Figure 3B–D), suggesting that GL1 and GL3 are essential for cortical localization of AGS.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing localization patterns of GL deletion mutants.

claim: GL1 deletion significantly reduced micromere formation.
source: The GL1 deletion significantly reduced micromere formation.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: GL2, GL3, or GL4 deletion showed no or little significant difference in micromere formation compared to Full AGS.
source: In contrast, the GL2, GL3, or GL4 deletion showed no or little significant difference in micromere formation compared to the Full AGS control group (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3F.

claim: GL1 deletion showed significant disruption in embryonic development at 2 dpf.
source: Consequently, the GL1 deletion showed significant disruption in embryonic development at 2 dpf, likely due to a lack of micromeres' inductive signaling at the 16-cell stage (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: GL1 is critical for both AGS localization and function at the vegetal cortex for micromere formation.
source: These results suggest GL1 is critical for both AGS localization and function at the vegetal cortex for micromere formation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing effects of GL1 deletion on localization and function.

claim: GL3 and GL4 are important for intramolecular binding to the TPR domain.
source: GL3 and GL4 are important for intramolecular binding to the TPR domain in other organisms, which may impact the proper open-close control of AGS protein (Du and Macara, 2004; Johnston et al., 2009; Nipper et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Du and Macara, 2004; Johnston et al., 2009; Nipper et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2013).

claim: AGS1111 and AGS2222 severely inhibited micromere formation.
source: Most embryos that formed micromeres displayed vegetal cortical localization for all mutants except for AGS1111 and AGS2222 that severely inhibited micromere formation (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: AGS2222 showed vegetal cortical localization in embryos that formed micromeres.
source: Among the embryos that formed micromeres, AGS2222 always showed vegetal cortical localization, suggesting that AGS localization and micromere formation are closely linked to each other.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: AGS localization and micromere formation are closely linked to each other.
source: Among the embryos that formed micromeres, AGS2222 always showed vegetal cortical localization, suggesting that AGS localization and micromere formation are closely linked to each other.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: AGS1111 and AGS2222 displayed ectopic cortical localization around the entire embryo.
source: Additionally, most of the AGS1111 (99.36% ± 0.64, n = 182) and AGS2222 embryos (98.06% ± 1.94, n = 170) displayed ectopic cortical localization around the entire embryo (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: AGS1111 and AGS2222 mutants failed to restore micromere formation.
source: AGS1111 and AGS2222 mutants failed to restore micromere formation at the 16-cell stage, while AGS4234 and AGS2134 mutants rescued micromere formation similarly to Full AGS (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 4D.

claim: AGS4234 and AGS2134 mutants rescued micromere formation similarly to Full AGS.
source: AGS1111 and AGS2222 mutants failed to restore micromere formation at the 16-cell stage, while AGS4234 and AGS2134 mutants rescued micromere formation similarly to Full AGS (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The GL1 sequence is not essential, but its position is vital.
source: These results suggest that the GL1 sequence is not essential, but its position is vital.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing effects of GL motif swapping.

claim: The sequence of GL3 or GL4 appears to be critical for restricting AGS localization to the vegetal cortex.
source: In contrast, the sequence of GL3 or GL4 appears to be critical for restricting AGS localization to the vegetal cortex, perhaps by maintaining the autoinhibited form of AGS through their interaction with the TPR domains.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing effects of GL motif swapping.

claim: AGS1111 and AGS2222 mutants were unable to sustain a closed/inactive state.
source: AGS1111 and AGS2222 mutants were thus unable to sustain a closed/inactive state, resulting in a constitutively active form all around the cortex.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations of localization patterns.

claim: AGS4444 localized properly at the vegetal cortex.
source: AGS4444 localized properly at the vegetal cortex, whereas AGS-GL1GL2 showed significantly fewer embryos with vegetal cortical localization (Figure 4H and I).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 4H and I.

claim: AGS-GL1GL2 showed significantly fewer embryos with vegetal cortical localization.
source: AGS4444 localized properly at the vegetal cortex, whereas AGS-GL1GL2 showed significantly fewer embryos with vegetal cortical localization (Figure 4H and I).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 4H and I.

claim: AGS-GL1GL2 showed impaired function in micromere formation and development.
source: Furthermore, AGS-GL1GL2 showed impaired function in micromere formation and development compared to Full AGS control (Figure 4J and K).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 4J and K.

claim: AGS4444 showed no significant difference in micromere formation and development compared to Full AGS.
source: On the other hand, AGS4444 showed no significant difference in the proportion of embryos with micromeres at the 16-cell stage and normal development at 2 dpf compared to the Full AGS control.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: GL3 and GL4 are essential for maintaining SpAGS in a closed conformation.
source: These results further support the hypothesis that GL3 and GL4 are essential for maintaining SpAGS in a closed conformation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing effects of GL motif modifications.

claim: The position of GL1 is critical for SpAGS localization and function.
source: Additionally, the position of GL1 is critical for SpAGS localization and function.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing effects of GL1 position changes.

claim: EtAGS showed no significant difference in localization and function compared to SpAGS.
source: EtAGS showed no significant difference in localization and function compared to the SpAGS control, whereas PmAGS failed in vegetal cortical localization and micromere formation and function (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5B–E.

claim: PmAGS failed in vegetal cortical localization and micromere formation and function.
source: EtAGS showed no significant difference in localization and function compared to the SpAGS control, whereas PmAGS failed in vegetal cortical localization and micromere formation and function (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5B–E.

claim: PmAGS is incapable of inducing micromere formation.
source: Hence, PmAGS is incapable of inducing micromere formation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: The N-terminal sequences of SpAGS and PmAGS are almost identical.
source: Since the N-terminal sequences of SpAGS and PmAGS are almost identical (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), we hypothesize that the variable C-terminus made a difference in AGS localization and function at the vegetal cortex.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Chimeras of ACD-facilitating orthologs (EtGL, LGNGL, DmGL) showed no significant difference in vegetal cortical localization and micromere function compared to SpAGS.
source: The chimeras of ACD-facilitating orthologs (EtGL, LGNGL, DmGL) showed no significant difference in the vegetal cortical localization and micromere function compared to the SpAGS control (Figure 5G–J).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5G–J.

claim: Chimeras of non-ACD-facilitators (AGS3GL and PmGL) failed in micromere formation and function.
source: In contrast, chimeras of non-ACD-facilitators (AGS3GL and PmGL) failed in micromere formation and function.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: The AGS C-terminus creates ACD diversity by primarily reflecting the original function of each ortholog in the host species.
source: These results suggest that the AGS C-terminus creates ACD diversity by primarily reflecting the original function of each ortholog in the host species.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing differential functions of chimeric AGS constructs.

claim: Drosophila Pins chimera (DmGL) showed reduced micromere formation.
source: Of note, Drosophila Pins chimera (DmGL) showed reduced micromere formation (Figure 5I), which may be due to fewer functional domains with decreased efficacy in the higher-order organism (Wavreil and Yajima, 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5I and supported by citation (Wavreil and Yajima, 2020).

claim: SbAGS signal at the vegetal cortex was significantly reduced compared to SpAGS.
source: In the resultant sea urchin embryos at the 16-cell stage, the SbAGS signal appeared slightly enriched on the asters and in the cytoplasm of micromeres. However, its signal at the vegetal cortex was significantly reduced compared to the 2x-GFP-SpAGS control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: SbAGS is less recruited to the vegetal cortex.
source: These results suggest that SbAGS is less recruited to the vegetal cortex.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: AGS-PmGL showed cortical localization yet still failed to facilitate ACD.
source: Another unexpected result obtained in this study is that AGS-PmGL showed cortical localization yet still failed to facilitate ACD (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5G–I.

claim: Vegetal cortical localization of AGS does not automatically grant its function in ACD.
source: This result suggests that vegetal cortical localization of AGS does not automatically grant its function in ACD.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations of AGS-PmGL.

claim: Aurora A phosphorylates the serine in the linker region of Pins, which recruits Pins to the cortex in Drosophila.
source: Indeed, it has been reported that Aurora A phosphorylates the serine in the linker region of Pins, which recruits Pins to the cortex and partially controls the spindle orientation in Drosophila (Johnston et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Johnston et al., 2009).

claim: SpAGS and EtAGS have predicted Aurora A phosphorylation site within the linker region, while PmAGS does not.
source: The phosphorylation site prediction algorithm GPS 6.0 (Chen et al., 2023) reveals that SpAGS and EtAGS have the predicted Aurora A phosphorylation site within the linker region, while PmAGS does not (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on computational prediction analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: AGS-S389A showed reduced vegetal cortical localization compared to Full AGS.
source: Compared to the Full AGS control, the mutant AGS-S389A showed reduced vegetal cortical localization (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D) and ACD function (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: PmAGS-SpLinker mutant did not restore cortical localization or proper function in ACD.
source: However, this mutant did not restore any cortical localization nor proper function in ACD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2H–K).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2H–K.

claim: Restoring the predicted Aurora A phosphorylation site is insufficient to induce cortical localization of AGS.
source: This result suggests that restoring the predicted Aurora A phosphorylation site is insufficient to induce the cortical localization of AGS.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations of PmAGS-SpLinker mutant.

claim: The chimera replaced with LGN residues (AGS3GL-GL2GL3) gained proper localization and function.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the chimera replaced with the LGN residues (AGS3GL-GL2GL3) gained the proper localization and function, while the chimera with serine alterations (AGS3GL-3S/A) failed to function in ACD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–F.

claim: The chimera with serine alterations (AGS3GL-3S/A) failed to function in ACD.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the chimera replaced with the LGN residues (AGS3GL-GL2GL3) gained the proper localization and function, while the chimera with serine alterations (AGS3GL-3S/A) failed to function in ACD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–F.

claim: Specific amino acid residues within the GL3 motif and between GL2-GL3 are critical for mediating interaction with TPR domains.
source: These results suggest that specific amino acid residues within the GL3 motif and between GL2-GL3 are critical, likely mediating interaction with TPR domains and the autoinhibited state of AGS.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing effects of specific amino acid mutations.

claim: Potential serine phosphorylation between GL2-GL3 motifs appears to be irrelevant to AGS function.
source: On the other hand, potential serine phosphorylation between GL2-GL3 motifs appears to be irrelevant to the AGS function.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations of serine mutation effects.

claim: The variable C-terminus of AGS orthologs primarily facilitates ACD diversity.
source: Overall, we conclude that the variable C-terminus of AGS orthologs primarily facilitates ACD diversity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental observations throughout the study.

claim: The N-terminus and linker region of AGS help mediate its autoinhibited state or recruitment.
source: At the same time, the N-terminus and the linker region of AGS appear to help mediate its autoinhibited state or recruitment, which regulates its cortical localization (summary diagrams in Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and summarized in Figure 6.

claim: ACD factors are enriched at the vegetal cortex during or upon micromere formation.
source: GFP live imaging or immunofluorescence of these ACD factors showed the highest signal enrichment at the vegetal cortex during or upon micromere formation, as well as on the spindle of all blastomeres to some extent (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Poon et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1, and supported by citation (Poon et al., 2019).

claim: ACD factors physically interact with AGS primarily at the vegetal cortex.
source: The results suggest these ACD factors physically interact with AGS primarily at the vegetal cortex (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is based on proximity ligation assay results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: AGS interacts with Vasa at the vegetal cortex.
source: We also observed AGS interacting with a fate determinant, Vasa, that is known to be enriched in micromeres at the vegetal cortex (Figure 7B; Voronina and Wessel, 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7B and supported by citation (Voronina and Wessel, 2006).

claim: AGS may recruit both ACD factors and fate determinants to the vegetal cortex.
source: These results indicate that AGS may recruit both ACD factors and fate determinants to the vegetal cortex, directly facilitating rapid lineage segregation of micromeres.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations of protein interactions.

claim: SpAGS knockdown reduced the signal enrichment of ACD factors and β-catenin.
source: Consistent with this observation, SpAGS knockdown reduced the signal enrichment of ACD factors and another fate determinant of micromeres, β-catenin (Logan et al., 1999; Figure 7C–H).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7C–H and supported by citation (Logan et al., 1999).

claim: SpAGS recruits the spindle poles to every cortex when overexpressed.
source: In our previous study (Poon et al., 2019), we also identified that SpAGS recruits the spindle poles to every cortex when overexpressed (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, arrows).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and supported by citation (Poon et al., 2019).

claim: SpAGS at least partially recruits its partner proteins to ectopic cortical regions.
source: Similarly, SpAGS at least partially recruits its partner proteins to the ectopic cortical region, which we never observed in the control group (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B and C, arrows).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: SpAGS directly recruits multiple ACD factors and fate determinants necessary for micromere formation and organizer function.
source: These results support the idea that SpAGS directly recruits the molecules essential for micromere lineage segregation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations of protein recruitment.

claim: Endomesoderm marker genes decreased their expression territories in AGS-knockdown embryos.
source: Indeed, in situ hybridization (ISH) analysis suggests that the downstream genes regulated by micromere signaling, such as endomesoderm marker genes (wnt8, foxa, blimp1b, and endo16), decreased their expression territories in the AGS-knockdown embryos (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Ectoderm and skeletogenic mesoderm marker genes showed no significant change in expression by AGS knockdown.
source: In contrast, ectoderm (foxq2) and skeletogenic mesoderm (ets1, alx1, tbr1, and sm50) marker genes showed no significant change in their expressions by AGS knockdown.
evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization analysis described in the manuscript.

claim: SpAGS functions as an organizer, facilitating downstream gene expressions necessary for endomesoderm specification.
source: Overall, these results suggest that SpAGS directly recruits multiple ACD factors and fate determinants necessary for micromere formation and functions as an organizer, facilitating the downstream gene expressions necessary for endomesoderm specification.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations of gene expression patterns.

claim: Pm and Et Insc and Dlg showed cortical localization at the vegetal cortex in sea urchin embryos.
source: Importantly, these Pm and Et ACD factors showed cortical localization at the vegetal cortex in the sea urchin embryo (Figure 9C–F).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 9C–F.

claim: Insc and Dlg might not be significant variable factors controlling ACD.
source: Therefore, Insc and Dlg might not be the significant variable factors controlling ACD.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations showing conserved localization of Insc and Dlg orthologs.

claim: Only SpAGS injection increased the formation of micromere-like cells in pencil urchin embryos.
source: Notably, only SpAGS injection increased the formation of micromere-like cells in the resultant pencil urchin embryos. In contrast, EtAGS and PmAGS showed no significant difference from the negative control (Vasa-mCherry only, Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 10B.

claim: SpAGS increases the frequency of micromere-like cell formation in pencil urchin embryos.
source: This result suggests that SpAGS increases the frequency of micromere-like cell formation in pencil urchin embryos.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations in pencil urchin embryos.

claim: SpAGS increased Vasa signal enrichment in micromere-like cells at the 16-cell stage in pencil urchin.
source: We observed that SpAGS increased the Vasa signal enrichment in micromere-like cells compared to the control (Vasa-mCherry only) at the 16-cell stage. On the other hand, other AGS orthologs showed no significant difference from the control (Figure 10C and D).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 10C and D.

claim: Nearly 80% of SpAGS-injected pencil urchin embryos showed co-enrichment of AGS and Vasa in micromere-like cells.
source: Nearly 80% (80.12% ± 3.75) of the SpAGS-injected embryos showed co-enrichment of AGS and Vasa in micromere-like cells, while the EtAGS and PmAGS groups showed only 49.2% ± 8.94 and 43.37% ± 3.94 enrichment, respectively (Figure 10E).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 10E.

claim: The SpAGS group showed earlier segregation of Vasa-positive cells at 1 dpf in pencil urchin.
source: Consistently, the SpAGS group showed the earlier segregation of Vasa-positive cells similar to sea urchin embryos at 1 dpf (Figure 10F and G), potentially accelerating the lineage segregation of the germline in the pencil urchin embryo.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 10F and G.

claim: The GL1 motif of SpAGS is key for its vegetal cortical localization and function in micromere formation.
source: This study demonstrates that the GL1 motif of SpAGS is key for its vegetal cortical localization and function in micromere formation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental observations throughout the study.

claim: The unique role of the GL1 motif appears to be conserved across organisms including Drosophila and humans.
source: Importantly, this unique role of the GL1 motif appears to be conserved across organisms. In Drosophila Pins and human LGN, GL1 is free from TPR binding, making it essential for the recruitment of Pins/LGN to the cortex (Nipper et al., 2007; Takayanagi et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Nipper et al., 2007; Takayanagi et al., 2019).

claim: The evolutionary introduction of the GL1 motif into SpAGS likely increased recruitment affinity to the vegetal cortex.
source: Thus, the evolutionary introduction of the GL1 motif into SpAGS likely increased recruitment affinity to the vegetal cortex, inducing ACD in the sea urchin embryo.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations and evolutionary analysis.

claim: The GL1 position rather than the sequence is essential for SpAGS function in ACD regulation.
source: The GL1 deletion significantly disrupted micromere formation, while its replacement with other GL motifs had no effect. Therefore, the GL1 position rather than the sequence is essential for SpAGS function in ACD regulation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing effects of GL1 deletion and replacement.

claim: The GL1 and GL2 of SbAGS are located too close to each other, compromising GL1's independence for recruitment.
source: First, the GL1 and GL2 of SbAGS are located too close to each other, compromising GL1's independence for recruitment. Indeed, the SpAGS-GL1GL2 mutant in which GL1 and GL2 are located next to each other showed compromised cortical localization and ACD function in the sea urchin embryo (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The distance between GL1 and GL2 might be critical for GL1 to function properly.
source: This suggests the distance between GL1 and GL2 might be critical for the GL1 to function properly.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations of GL1GL2 mutant.

claim: A lack of GL4 in SbAGS loosens the autoinhibition state.
source: Second, a lack of GL4 in SbAGS loosens the autoinhibition state. The SpAGS mutant that lacks GL4 partially compromised ACD (Figure 3F), suggesting that the presence of GL4 is critical for ACD.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3F.

claim: In Drosophila Pins and human LGN, GL2-3 and GL3-4 sequences are essential for intramolecular interactions with TPR motifs.
source: In Drosophila Pins and human LGN, GL2-3 and GL3-4 sequences, respectively, are essential for their intramolecular interactions with TPR motifs, which control Pins/LGN's autoinhibited conformation (Nipper et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2013; Smith and Prehoda, 2011; Takayanagi et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Nipper et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2013; Smith and Prehoda, 2011; Takayanagi et al., 2019).

claim: Gαi binding to GL1 relieves autoinhibition to activate Pins/LGN.
source: Therefore, Gαi binding to GL1 relieves autoinhibition to activate them (Du and Macara, 2004; Nipper et al., 2007; Takayanagi et al., 2019; Pan et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Du and Macara, 2004; Nipper et al., 2007; Takayanagi et al., 2019; Pan et al., 2013).

claim: The constitutively open state of SpAGS mutants interacts with other ACD factors in an uncontrolled manner.
source: Presumably, the constitutively open state of these SpAGS mutants interacts with other ACD factors in an uncontrolled manner, resulting in abnormal polarity induction in the embryo.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from experimental observations of mutant phenotypes.

claim: Fine control of SpAGS close/open conformation is essential for accurate ACD regulation.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that fine control of SpAGS close/open conformation is essential for accurate ACD regulation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations of various mutants.

claim: Aurora A phosphorylation at the Pins' linker domain partially controls spindle orientation at the cortex.
source: A previous study suggests that Aurora A phosphorylation at the Pins' linker domain partially controls the spindle orientation at the cortex (Johnston et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Johnston et al., 2009).

claim: Cortical localization of Pins is insufficient and requires Dlg and Insc to control spindle orientation.
source: Further, a recent study suggests that cortical localization of Pins is insufficient and requires Dlg and Insc to control spindle orientation (Neville et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Neville et al., 2023).

claim: Pins could be recruited through the linker domain to the cortex while remaining inactive.
source: These studies suggest that Pins could be recruited through the linker domain to the cortex while remaining inactive.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cited literature.

claim: The SpAGS-PmGL mutant was recruited through the SpLinker domain while remaining inactive.
source: Therefore, we speculate the SpAGS-PmGL mutant that contains the SpLinker domain was recruited through this domain while remaining inactive in this study, which needs to be further tested in the future.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from experimental observations and literature.

claim: Micromere function as organizers might require additional changes in the developmental program of the entire embryo.
source: Although such lineage segregation of micromeres may be mediated solely by ACD, their function as organizers might require additional changes in the developmental program of the entire embryo.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from experimental observations.

claim: Sea urchin embryos have a robust hyaline layer to keep blastomeres together.
source: For example, sea urchin embryos have a robust hyaline layer to keep blastomeres together, which presumably increases the cell–cell interaction and may also enhance cell signaling during early embryogenesis.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about sea urchin embryology.

claim: A hyaline layer is not or little present in sea star or pencil urchin embryos.
source: In contrast, a hyaline layer is not or little present in sea star or pencil urchin embryos, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about echinoderm embryology.

claim: The GL1 motif was once lost in the echinoderm common ancestor and recovered during sea urchin diversification.
source: Since the unique role of the GL1 motif appears to be conserved across organisms, including Drosophila and humans, it is possible that the GL1 motif was once lost in the echinoderm common ancestor and recovered during sea urchin diversification.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from evolutionary analysis and experimental observations.

claim: The recovery of the GL1 motif resumed the interaction between SpAGS and other ACD machinery at the cortex.
source: The recovery of this GL1 motif also resumed the interaction between SpAGS and other ACD machinery, such as NuMA, Insc, and Dlg, at the cortex in a similar manner to its orthologs Pins and LGN in other phyla, resulting in the controlled ACD and further interactions with fate determinants to form a new cell type in the sea urchin embryo.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from experimental observations and evolutionary analysis.

claim: AGS-mediated cell divisions appear to be highly organized and may be programmed to cause cell fate changes.
source: Therefore, unlike random unequal cell divisions that do not alter cell fates, AGS-mediated cell divisions appear to be highly organized and may be programmed to cause cell fate changes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations throughout the study.

claim: AGS is a variable factor in facilitating ACD diversity among echinoderm embryos.
source: Considering significant variations within the C-terminus of AGS orthologs and their immediate impact on micromere formation, we propose that AGS is a variable factor in facilitating ACD diversity among echinoderm embryos, contributing to developmental diversity within a phylum.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations and evolutionary analysis throughout the study.
